page.title: videocall.rs: how a call works, mapped

slots.overviewDescription: videocall.rs in context: who connects, the browser app, the two kinds of server and the message bus between them.
slots.mapDescription: The browser client, the Meeting API, the media servers and NATS, with the paths a join, a connection and a video frame take.
slots.completionIntro: You followed a participant from sign-in to a room token, through the transport election, and one video frame from a camera to another screen.
slots.completionLessons:
• Why there are two servers: one that decides who may join and one that only relays bytes
  • How a signed room token is the only link between them
  • Why media servers never talk to each other, only to NATS
  • How the client picks WebTransport or WebSocket by measuring round-trip time

panels.introHtml:
Start here

videocall.rs, a video conferencing system in Rust

A map of security-union/videocall-rs at commit 31a8b20, in C4 terms: context on this overview, containers and their main components on the full map. It favours the runtime model: how a call is set up and how media gets from one client to another.

The short version: a browser app written in Rust (WebAssembly) asks a small REST service for permission to join a room, then opens a WebSocket or WebTransport connection to a media server. Media servers do not mix or transcode anything. They relay protobuf packets through NATS to everyone else in the room. There is no WebRTC.

videocall.rs is made by Security Union LLC and contributors and released under the MIT or Apache 2.0 licence. This map describes it in its own words and is not affiliated with its authors.

Try it

  • Open a card to see its part of the system.
  • Play One video frame, from Alice to Bob to follow media through the servers.
  • Click a component for what it does and where it lives in the code.
panels.overviewHtml:
The full map

A control plane, a data plane and a bus

In the local dev stack (nix/dev-stack.nix) these run as separate processes: the browser app, the Meeting API (meeting-api, port 8081), two media servers built from one crate (actix-api: WebSocket on 8080, WebTransport on UDP 4433), two small metrics servers, NATS and PostgreSQL.

How to read it

People and clients on the left, servers in the middle, NATS and storage on the right. The browser zone and the media-server zone are opened up into their main components. Four cards have a look-inside view: the connection manager, the session actor, the room router and the wire format.

Component names inside a zone are Rust modules or actors, not processes.

people.title: People and devices
people.text: Most participants use the web app. The repository also holds native clients that speak the same protocol over WebTransport: a command-line streamer, a load-test bot and an FFI library for the mobile apps.

browser.title: Browser app
browser.line1: A Rust UI compiled to WebAssembly
browser.line2: and a client library under it.
browser.text: The UI (Dioxus) handles pages, sign-in and the waiting room. Under it, videocall-client owns the connection, encodes camera, microphone and screen, decodes every peer and measures quality.

control.title: Meeting API
control.text: The control plane. It signs users in, stores meetings and participants, runs the waiting room and hands out short-lived room tokens. It never touches media.

media.title: Media servers
media.text: The data plane. One crate builds a WebSocket server and a WebTransport server. Both validate the room token, run one actor per connection and pass packets to and from NATS.

backbone.title: Message backbone
backbone.text: Every packet is a protobuf PacketWrapper, and every room is a family of NATS subjects. This pair is the contract all the other parts share.

observe.title: Observability
observe.text: Clients report what they receive from each peer. Two small servers read those reports from NATS and expose them for Prometheus to scrape.

outside.title: Identity provider
outside.line2: Google or Okta buttons in the UI.
outside.text: When OAuth is configured, the Meeting API sends people to an outside identity provider and turns the result into its own session cookie.

zones.label: Browser tab · Rust compiled to WebAssembly

nodes.what: Opens a meeting link, picks a display name and devices, and talks. The first person to join a new meeting id becomes its host; later joiners may have to wait to be admitted.
nodes.why: Everything else exists to move this person's camera, microphone and screen to the other people in the room with little delay.
nodes.tools: A browser with WebCodecs. The UI checks for MediaStreamTrackProcessor and VideoEncoder and turns Firefox away unless firefoxEnabled is set (dioxus-ui/src/components/browser_compatibility.rs). WebTransport is not required: the client tries both transports and keeps one.

nodes.what: Programs that join a room without a browser. videocall-cli streams a camera or test pattern from a desktop, robot or Raspberry Pi. bot sends recorded audio and video for load tests. videocall-sdk wraps a WebTransport client behind UniFFI bindings meant for iOS and Android; the app projects under apps/ are still template stubs that do not call it.
nodes.why: They show the protocol is not tied to the browser: anything that can open a WebTransport session and send PacketWrapper bytes is a participant.
nodes.tools: web-transport-quinn · the VP9 encoder in videocall-codecs (pure Rust by default, libvpx as an opt-in feature) · UniFFI. Key files: videocall-cli/src/consumers/webtransport.rs, bot/src/webtransport_client.rs, videocall-sdk/src/lib.rs. The CLI and the bot connect with the older /lobby/USER/ROOM path, which the server accepts only when FEATURE_MEETING_MANAGEMENT is off.

nodes.what: An outside sign-in service. The Meeting API redirects the browser to it, then exchanges the returned code for tokens and reads the user's email and name.
nodes.why: Optional. With no OAUTH_CLIENT_ID the login routes answer with an error; separately, the UI skips its session check when its own oauthEnabled setting is off. Not visible in the code: how a person gets a session cookie in that mode; the end-to-end tests inject a signed cookie themselves (e2e/helpers/auth.ts).
nodes.tools: Any OIDC provider; endpoints come from OAUTH_ISSUER discovery or explicit URLs (meeting-api/src/config.rs, meeting-api/src/oauth.rs). The UI has Google and Okta sign-in buttons.

nodes.what: The pages and components: home, meeting, settings, the waiting room, peer tiles and host controls. It calls the Meeting API through videocall-meeting-client and, once it holds a room token, builds the lobby URLs and creates a VideoCallClient.
nodes.why: It is the only part that knows about meetings as a product (hosts, waiting, admission). The client library below it only knows rooms, peers and packets.
nodes.tools: Dioxus 0.7 for the web, built with Trunk; runtime settings come from window.__APP_CONFIG in dioxus-ui/scripts/config.js. Key files: dioxus-ui/src/pages/meeting.rs (join state machine), dioxus-ui/src/components/attendants.rs (creates the call client), dioxus-ui/src/components/waiting_room.rs (creates an observer client, as the meeting page does while waiting for the host), videocall-meeting-client/src/. Log records at warning level and above are also sent to a Matomo analytics server through the matomo-logger crate (dioxus-ui/src/main.rs).

nodes.what: The hub of the client library. It owns the connection controller, the peer decode manager and the optional end-to-end encryption keys, and it sorts every inbound PacketWrapper by type: media to the decoders, MEETING events to UI callbacks, DIAGNOSTICS to the sender-side controller, CONGESTION to a step-down flag.
nodes.why: One place decides what each packet type means for the client, so the UI and the encoders never parse the envelope themselves.
nodes.tools: Rust for wasm32-unknown-unknown. Key file: videocall-client/src/client/video_call_client.rs (on_inbound_media). End-to-end encryption is off unless e2eeEnabled is set. When on, each client sends its RSA public key whenever it first sees a new peer; a client that receives one answers with its own AES-128-CBC key encrypted to that public key, and both packets are relayed through the servers like any other (RSA_PUB_KEY, AES_KEY). Code: videocall-client/src/crypto/.

nodes.what: Opens a connection to every configured server URL at once, measures round-trip time on each, elects one and closes the rest. After that it sends heartbeats, keeps probing once a second, starts a new election if latency degrades and reconnects with backoff when the link drops.
nodes.why: A client cannot know in advance whether WebTransport works on its network or which region is closest. Measuring is cheaper than guessing.
nodes.tools: Browser WebSocket and WebTransport APIs through videocall-transport. Key files: videocall-client/src/connection/connection_manager.rs, connection_controller.rs (timers), connection.rs (heartbeat), webtransport.rs and websocket.rs.

nodes.what: Three capture pipelines: camera, microphone and screen share. Video frames go through the browser's WebCodecs VideoEncoder (VP9, or VP8 on Firefox); audio goes through an Opus encoder worklet. Each encoded chunk becomes a MediaPacket with a sequence number, is encrypted if end-to-end encryption is on, and is wrapped as a MEDIA packet.
nodes.why: Encoding happens in the browser because the servers never look inside media. The sequence number is what lets a receiver notice a gap and ask for a keyframe.
nodes.tools: WebCodecs, MediaStreamTrackProcessor, AudioWorklet. Key files: videocall-client/src/encode/camera_encoder.rs, microphone_encoder.rs, screen_encoder.rs, transform.rs (video chunk to packet; the audio equivalent is in microphone_encoder.rs).

nodes.what: Keeps one entry per remote session with a video decoder, a screen decoder and an audio decoder. Video packets go to a web worker that holds a jitter buffer and a WebCodecs VideoDecoder, and decoded frames are drawn on a canvas. Audio packets go to a second worker running NetEq, an adaptive jitter buffer, and come back as PCM for playback.
nodes.why: Packets arrive late, in bursts or not at all. The jitter buffers trade a little delay for smooth playback, and gap tracking turns a lost video frame into a keyframe request instead of a frozen picture.
nodes.tools: Key files: videocall-client/src/decode/peer_decode_manager.rs, peer_decoder.rs, neteq_audio_decoder.rs. The workers come from two other crates: videocall-codecs/src/bin/worker_decoder.rs and neteq/src/bin/neteq_worker.rs.

nodes.what: Measures what the client receives from each peer (frame rate, bitrate) and sends it two ways: a DIAGNOSTICS packet to the peers, and a HEALTH packet meant for the servers' metrics. On the sending side it turns the diagnostics it gets back into a target bitrate and a quality tier for the encoders.
nodes.why: There is no server-side bandwidth estimation. Receivers tell senders how it is going, and senders adapt. The one server-made signal is CONGESTION, sent when a receiver's outbound queue overflows.
nodes.tools: Key files: videocall-client/src/diagnostics/diagnostics_manager.rs, encoder_bitrate_controller.rs, adaptive_quality_manager.rs, videocall-client/src/health_reporter.rs. The UI turns both on with a 1 second diagnostics interval and a 5 second health interval.

nodes.what: A REST service for sign-in and meetings: OAuth login and callback, session check, meeting create, list, end and delete, join and leave, and the waiting room (list, admit, reject). Joining returns either a room token or an observer token. It also publishes meeting events to NATS (activation, waiting room changes, admit, reject) so waiting clients are told at once. Leaving or ending a meeting updates the database only; nothing is published for those.
nodes.why: It is the only issuer of room tokens. A media server accepts a connection only with a token signed with the same JWT_SECRET, so who may join is decided here and nowhere else.
nodes.tools: Axum 0.8, sqlx, jsonwebtoken (HMAC), async-nats; listens on 0.0.0.0:8081 by default. Key files: meeting-api/src/routes/mod.rs (route table), routes/participants.rs (join), routes/waiting_room.rs, token.rs, auth.rs, nats_events.rs. Room tokens live 60 seconds by default (TOKEN_TTL_SECS); observer tokens 30 minutes. GET /api/v1/versions also fetches /version from the URLs in SERVICE_VERSION_URLS, typically the media servers.

nodes.what: Holds the meeting state: meetings (room id, creator, state idle, active or ended, waiting room on or off), meeting_participants (status waiting, admitted, rejected or left, host flag, display name), users and the short-lived oauth_requests rows used during login.
nodes.why: Meetings and admissions must outlive any one server process. Media servers keep nothing here: in the dev stack they run with DATABASE_ENABLED=false.
nodes.tools: PostgreSQL in the dev stack and Helm charts; the Meeting API can also be built for SQLite (sqlite feature). Schema and migrations: dbmate/db/migrations/, dbmate/db/schema.sql; queries: meeting-api/src/db/.

nodes.what: An Actix Web server whose main route is GET /lobby?token=JWT. It validates the room token, reads user, room, display name and observer flag from the claims, and upgrades the request to a WebSocket handled by a session actor. Frames up to 4 MB are accepted.
nodes.why: WebSocket works in every browser and through most proxies, so it is the transport that always exists.
nodes.tools: actix-web 4, actix-web-actors; port from ACTIX_PORT (8080). Key files: actix-api/src/bin/websocket_server.rs, actix-api/src/lobby.rs, actix-api/src/token_validator.rs. The same binary still carries an older cookie-based OAuth login, registered only when OAuth and the database are both configured.

nodes.what: A QUIC endpoint that accepts WebTransport sessions on /lobby?token=JWT, validates the same token, and bridges each session to a session actor: one task reads unidirectional streams, one reads datagrams and one writes. A small HTTP server beside it answers health checks.
nodes.why: QUIC streams are independent, so one lost packet does not hold up everything behind it as it does on a single TCP connection. The client prefers this transport when it works.
nodes.tools: quinn and web-transport-quinn, TLS 1.3 with certificates from CERT_PATH and KEY_PATH; listens on LISTEN_URL (UDP 4433 in dev). Key files: actix-api/src/bin/webtransport_server.rs, actix-api/src/webtransport/mod.rs, actix-api/src/webtransport/bridge.rs.

nodes.what: One actor per client connection: WsChatSession or WtChatSession, both thin wrappers around the shared SessionLogic. It gets a random 64-bit session id, tells the client that id, classifies every inbound packet (echo an RTT probe, drop, publish as health, rate-limit a keyframe request, or forward to the room) and writes outbound packets to the socket.
nodes.why: Keeping the decisions in one transport-neutral struct means the two transports cannot drift apart in behaviour.
nodes.tools: Key files: actix-api/src/actors/session_logic.rs, actix-api/src/actors/packet_handler.rs, actix-api/src/actors/transports/ws_chat_session.rs, wt_chat_session.rs. Clients are dropped after 30 seconds of silence (actix-api/src/constants.rs).

nodes.what: The room router. It keeps the sessions on this process, their state (Testing or Active) and who is in which room. On join it subscribes that session to the room's NATS subjects; on each forwarded packet it publishes to the session's own subject; on each NATS message it hands the bytes to the right session actor. It also announces joins, and leaves after a 2 second grace period (PARTICIPANT_LEFT on the system subject).
nodes.why: It owns every room subscription and almost all publishing on room.* subjects; the exceptions there are CONGESTION signals, which session actors publish themselves, and meeting events from the Meeting API. Health reports and server connection events use other subjects and other publishers. Because every delivery goes through NATS, two people in a room can be on different servers, or different transports, without either server knowing.
nodes.tools: actix, async-nats. Key file: actix-api/src/actors/chat_server.rs; subject builder in actix-api/src/models/mod.rs.

nodes.what: Carries every packet between server processes. Subjects in use: room.ROOM.SESSION for packets from one sender, room.ROOM.system for meeting events, health.diagnostics.REGION.SERVICE.SERVER for client health reports and server.connections.REGION.SERVICE.SERVER for server connection events.
nodes.why: Without it a room would be limited to one server process. With it, media servers stay independent of each other and can be added or removed freely.
nodes.tools: nats-server (started with JetStream enabled in the dev stack, though the code shown here uses plain publish and subscribe); clients use the async-nats crate. Dev setup: nix/dev-stack.nix; Helm values under helm/global/.

nodes.what: The protobuf messages every part speaks. A PacketWrapper envelope carries a type, the sender's user id and session id, and an opaque payload; the payload is a MediaPacket, a MeetingPacket, a HealthPacket and so on depending on the type.
nodes.why: Servers route on the envelope alone and can relay payloads they cannot read, which is what makes end-to-end encryption possible.
nodes.tools: Definitions in protobuf/types/; generated Rust checked in under videocall-types/src/protos/ (regenerate with protobuf/Makefile). Used by the client, both servers, the Meeting API and the native clients.

nodes.what: Two NATS consumers that expose Prometheus text on /metrics. metrics_server reads client health reports from health.diagnostics.> and turns them into per-session, per-peer gauges. metrics_server_snapshot reads server.connections.> events that each media server publishes about its connections and bytes.
nodes.why: Health data arrives at whichever media server a client happens to use. Publishing it to NATS and aggregating here gives one scrape target per kind of metric.
nodes.tools: actix-web, prometheus crate, async-nats; ports from METRICS_PORT (9091 and 9092 in dev). Key files: actix-api/src/bin/metrics_server.rs, actix-api/src/bin/metrics_server_snapshot.rs, actix-api/src/server_diagnostics.rs.

nodes.what: Prometheus scrapes the two metrics servers; Grafana shows dashboards built on those series.
nodes.why: Call quality problems are per person and per network. These dashboards are how operators see them without access to anyone's media.
nodes.tools: Scrape config and alert rules in monitoring/prometheus/, dashboards in monitoring/grafana/; both run in the dev stack and have Helm values under helm/global/.

join.title: Sign in and join as host
join.desc: Alice opens a meeting link. The Meeting API signs her in, creates the meeting with her as host and returns a room token.

hops.t: Alice opens /meeting/standup. With OAuth on, the meeting page first asks the Meeting API whether she has a session (GET /session); if not, it remembers the URL and shows the login page (dioxus-ui/src/pages/meeting.rs).
The login button points the browser at GET /login on the Meeting API, which creates a PKCE challenge, a CSRF state and a nonce.
Those three values are stored in oauth_requests so the callback can be checked against them (meeting-api/src/routes/oauth.rs).
The browser is redirected to the identity provider. On return, GET /login/callback exchanges the code for tokens, verifies the ID token and reads the email and name.
The user is upserted and the API answers with a redirect back to the meeting URL plus a session JWT in an HttpOnly cookie. From here on every API call carries that cookie.
Alice picks a display name and the page sends POST /api/v1/meetings/standup/join.
No meeting called standup exists, so one is created with Alice as creator. As host she activates it and gets a participant row with status admitted (meeting-api/src/routes/participants.rs).
Activation is published as a MEETING_ACTIVATED event on room.standup.system, in case someone is already waiting for the host. If NATS is not configured this step is skipped.
The response carries a room token: a JWT with her user id, the room, room_join: true, is_host: true and a 60 second expiry by default. It is only needed to open the connection.
The page switches to the call view, which builds /lobby?token=… URLs for every configured server and creates a VideoCallClient (dioxus-ui/src/components/attendants.rs).

connect.title: Connect and elect a transport
connect.desc: The client connects to every server it knows, measures round-trip time and keeps one connection. The server announces the participant only once that connection is used.

hops.t: The UI passes two URL lists from config.js: WebSocket servers and WebTransport servers. Each list may name several servers, for example one per region.
The connection manager starts an election and opens a connection to every URL at the same time.

WebSocket: GET /lobby?token=JWT. The server checks signature, expiry and issuer, rejects room names that are not NATS-safe, and requires room_join or observer. A bad token gets 401 or 403 before any upgrade.
WebTransport, in parallel and only if enabled in the UI config: a QUIC handshake, then the same path and the same token check.
Each accepted connection gets its own session actor with a fresh 64-bit session id. On start it sends two packets straight back: SESSION_ASSIGNED with that id, and MEETING_STARTED.
The actor registers with ChatServer, which marks the session Testing, and then sends JoinRoom.
ChatServer subscribes the session to room.standup.* and sends it one PARTICIPANT_JOINED per person already in the room. Nothing is announced about the newcomer yet.
During the election the client sends an RTT probe on every connection every 200 ms. A probe is a MEDIA packet of type RTT carrying a timestamp.
The session actor echoes each probe to its sender and nowhere else. The client averages the last ten round trips per connection.

After the election period (2 seconds by default, extended by a second at most twice while no connection has two samples) the client picks, in order: the fastest WebTransport connection with at least two samples, the fastest WebSocket connection with at least two, then connections with a single sample. The others are closed.
The winner starts sending a heartbeat every 5 seconds with camera, microphone and screen state. The first packet that is not an RTT probe makes the session actor send ActivateConnection.
ChatServer moves the session from Testing to Active. Only Active sessions may publish to the room.
Now the join is announced: PARTICIPANT_JOINED goes out on room.standup.system. The losing connections never became Active, so nobody saw them.

media.title: One video frame, from Alice to Bob
media.desc: A camera frame is encoded in Alice's browser, relayed by her server through NATS to Bob's server, and decoded in Bob's browser. No server decodes it.

hops.t: Alice's camera frame is encoded by the browser's VideoEncoder (VP9). The chunk becomes a MediaPacket with type VIDEO and a sequence number, is AES-encrypted if end-to-end encryption is on, and is wrapped in a PacketWrapper of type MEDIA.
send_media_packet hands it to the elected connection.
On WebTransport each media packet travels on its own unidirectional stream; small control packets go as datagrams. On WebSocket it would be one binary frame.
The bridge reads the stream (up to 4 MB) and passes the bytes to Alice's session actor.
The actor classifies the packet. It is ordinary media from a non-observer, so it is forwarded to ChatServer as a ClientMessage.
ChatServer stamps Alice's session id into the envelope and publishes the bytes to room.standup.ALICE_SESSION.

Every session in the room has a subscription to room.standup.*, on whichever server process it lives. Bob's subscription receives the message; Alice's own subscription skips it because the subject is hers.
The bytes are handed to Bob's session actor. If its mailbox is full the packet is dropped and the subscription carries on.
Bob is on WebSocket, so his actor writes one binary frame. Had he been on WebTransport, a full outbound queue would count as a drop against Alice's session and could trigger a CONGESTION signal.
Bob's browser receives the frame on its elected connection.
VideoCallClient sees a MEDIA packet from a session id it may not know yet and creates the peer if needed.

The peer's decoder decrypts and parses the MediaPacket, checks the sequence number for gaps, and posts the frame to the video worker, where a jitter buffer feeds a WebCodecs VideoDecoder. The decoded frame is drawn on Bob's canvas for Alice.

waiting.title: Waiting room: knock and be admitted
waiting.desc: Bob joins a meeting that has the waiting room on. He gets an observer token, listens on the media server for news, and receives his room token only after the host admits him.

hops.t: Bob sends POST /api/v1/meetings/standup/join. He is not the creator and the meeting is active.
In one transaction the API reads waiting_room_enabled and inserts Bob with status waiting. With the waiting room off he would be admitted here and get a room token at once.
A WAITING_ROOM_UPDATED event on room.standup.system tells the host's client to refresh its list of people waiting.
Bob's response has no room token. It has an observer token instead: same room, room_join: false, observer: true, valid for 30 minutes.
The waiting room component creates a VideoCallClient with the observer token, diagnostics and health reporting off.
It connects like any client. The media server marks the session as observer: it receives room traffic, cannot publish media, and is never announced as a participant.
Meanwhile the host clicks Admit, and her UI sends POST /api/v1/meetings/standup/admit with Bob's user id. The API checks that the caller is the admitted host.
Bob's row changes to admitted.
The API publishes PARTICIPANT_ADMITTED with target_user_id set to Bob. The token is deliberately not in the broadcast.
Bob's observer session is subscribed to room.standup.*, so the event reaches his server process.
It travels down his observer connection as a MEETING packet.
VideoCallClient compares target_user_id with its own user id and fires the admitted callback into the waiting room component.

The component calls GET /api/v1/meetings/standup/status, which now includes a room token, and the page moves on to the call view. The component also polls the same endpoint every 5 seconds the whole time, as a safety net in case the push is missed.

feedback.title: Quality feedback and metrics
feedback.desc: Receivers report what they get. One report goes to the sender to steer its encoder, another to the metrics servers. The media server adds its own signal when a receiver cannot keep up.

hops.t: Each decoded packet is counted per peer and media type, giving received frame rate and bitrate.
Two kinds of report leave Bob's client: DIAGNOSTICS packets about each sender, and a HEALTH packet every 5 seconds summarising all peers, the active server and its RTT.
Both travel on the elected connection like any other packet.
The session actor recognises HEALTH and does not relay it to the room. It publishes it to health.diagnostics.REGION.SERVICE.SERVER instead.
metrics_server consumes that subject family in a queue group and updates Prometheus gauges per session and peer.
Prometheus scrapes /metrics; Grafana dashboards read from Prometheus.
DIAGNOSTICS packets, by contrast, are ordinary room traffic and are relayed to everyone, including the sender they describe.
Alice's VideoCallClient passes each DIAGNOSTICS packet to her sender-side diagnostics.
Her encoder bitrate controller turns the reported frame rates into a new target bitrate, and the adaptive quality manager moves between quality tiers when that is not enough.

A separate, server-made signal: when a WebTransport session's outbound queue (256 messages) is full and 5 packets from one sender are dropped within a second, the receiver's session publishes a CONGESTION packet on that sender's subject, at most once a second per sender. Clients cannot forge it; a CONGESTION packet arriving from a client is dropped.
Alice's client sees CONGESTION addressed to her session id and sets a flag that makes her encoder step down a quality tier.

buildSteps.title: One room, one server
buildSteps.text: A client, a socket, and a server that hands every packet from one connection to the others in the same room.
buildSteps.decision: Packets are one protobuf envelope with a type and an opaque payload, so the server can route without understanding media.

buildSteps.title: Put a bus between servers
buildSteps.text: Publish every packet to a NATS subject for its room and deliver from a subscription, even when sender and receiver share a process.
buildSteps.decision: Servers never talk to each other. A room is a subject pattern, so adding a server needs no configuration.

buildSteps.title: Real media
buildSteps.text: Encode camera, microphone and screen in the browser; decode each peer behind a jitter buffer.
buildSteps.decision: Use the browser's WebCodecs encoder and decoder and keep the relay codec-agnostic, instead of adopting WebRTC.

buildSteps.title: A faster transport, chosen by measurement
buildSteps.text: Add a WebTransport server next to the WebSocket one and let the client race them.
buildSteps.decision: Both transports share one session logic struct; the client elects by round-trip time and prefers WebTransport.

buildSteps.title: Meetings, identity and tokens
buildSteps.text: A separate REST service owns sign-in, hosts, the waiting room and admission, and signs short-lived room tokens.
buildSteps.decision: The media servers stay stateless: they trust a signed token and never query the database.

buildSteps.title: Measure and adapt
buildSteps.text: Receivers report quality to senders and to the metrics pipeline; senders adjust bitrate and tier.
buildSteps.decision: Adaptation is driven by receivers, with one server-made congestion signal as a backstop.

tour.title: Video calls without WebRTC
body: videocall.rs is a video conferencing system written almost entirely in Rust, in the browser as well as on the server.
Seen from outside: people open a web app, the app asks a Meeting API for permission, then exchanges media through relay servers that are tied together by NATS.
tour.why: The usual stack hides transport, congestion control and codecs inside WebRTC. Here each of those is ordinary code you can read, which is why a map helps.

tour.title: Signing in
body: Follow Alice from a meeting link to a session cookie. This part is skipped when OAuth is off.
tour.why: The Meeting API issues its own session JWT after the identity provider vouches for the user, so the rest of the system depends on one secret, not on a provider.

tour.title: Joining returns a token, not a connection
body: The join call creates or finds the meeting and answers with a signed room token.
tour.why: That token is the only thing the media servers trust. It lives for a minute by default because it is only needed to open the connection.

tour.title: Connect to everything
body: The client opens a connection to every server it was given. Each server validates the token and gives the connection a session id.
tour.why: The connection is real but silent: the server holds it in a Testing state and tells nobody.

tour.title: Elect one, announce once
body: Round-trip probes decide which connection survives. The first real packet on it makes the participant visible.
tour.why: Announcing at activation rather than at connect is what stops the losing connections from showing up as ghost participants.

tour.title: One frame across the system
body: Encoded in one browser, relayed as opaque bytes through a session actor, NATS and another session actor, decoded in another browser.
tour.why: The servers are a relay, not a mixer. Cost per room grows with packets forwarded, not with video processing, and end-to-end encryption stays possible.

tour.title: The waiting room uses the same pipes
body: An observer token lets a waiting client sit on the media server and hear the moment it is admitted.
tour.why: The control plane has no socket to clients of its own. It reaches them by publishing to the room's system subject.

tour.title: How the call watches itself
body: Receivers measure and report; senders adapt; health reports become metrics.
tour.why: With no media processing on the server, the clients are the only place quality can be measured.

body: A control plane that issues tokens, a data plane that relays packets, and a bus that lets any number of relay servers act as one.
To go deeper, open the look-inside views on the connection manager, the session actor, ChatServer and the wire format.

session.title: Inside a session actor: one inbound packet
session.sub: What happens to each packet a client sends, in order. The WebSocket and WebTransport actors both call SessionLogic::handle_inbound and then act on its answer.
session.cap: The envelope is parsed once; for MEDIA packets the inner MediaPacket is parsed too, only to spot RTT probes and keyframe requests. If the payload is encrypted that inner parse fails and the packet is treated as ordinary data.

steps.d: A WebSocket binary frame, or a WebTransport stream or datagram. The liveness timer is reset.
Sent to the server diagnostics tracker over a channel.

steps.t: Classify by parsing the envelope once
steps.d: Returns Rtt, Health, KeyframeRequest, Dropped or Data. Bytes that do not parse count as Data.

steps.t: A CONGESTION packet from a client?
steps.d: Only servers may create these.
A MEDIA packet whose inner type is RTT.

exit.t: Echoed to the sender only; does not activate the session

steps.d: Published to NATS for the metrics servers on a spawned task.

exit.t: Goes to health.diagnostics.*, never to the room

steps.d: Ignored from observers and limited to 2 per second per session; otherwise forwarded.
Observer sessions (waiting room) may listen but not publish.

steps.t: First packet that is not an RTT probe: activate
steps.d: Sends ActivateConnection to ChatServer once per session. Any outcome other than an echo counts, including a packet that was dropped above.
The bytes are wrapped in a ClientMessage with session id, user and room.

chat.title: Inside ChatServer: join a room, then relay
chat.sub: The life of one session as ChatServer sees it: registered, joined, activated, publishing and receiving, then gone. Each step is a message handler in chat_server.rs.
chat.cap: Delivery always goes through NATS, even between two sessions on the same process. A departure is announced only after a 2 second grace period, so a quick reconnect by the same user causes neither a leave nor a join. The code can also publish MEETING_ENDED when a host leaves, but SessionManager::end_session currently always reports that the meeting continues.

steps.d: Stores the actor's address and marks the session Testing.

steps.t: JoinRoom: refuse the reserved system user id

steps.d: A pending departure for the same room and user is cancelled, and the join announcement is suppressed.
Non-observers are added to the room's member list; the list as it was is kept for the next steps.

steps.t: First in the room: publish MEETING_STARTED
steps.d: On room.ROOM.system, from a spawned task.

steps.t: Tell the newcomer who is already here
steps.d: One PARTICIPANT_JOINED per existing member, sent straight to the new session, not through NATS.
A queue subscription named after the session and room; the task then loops over incoming messages for the life of the session.
Publishes the deferred PARTICIPANT_JOINED on the system subject, unless this is a reconnect or an observer.

steps.t: Stamp the session id and publish
steps.d: If the envelope has no session id the server writes its own, then publishes to room.ROOM.SESSION.
Messages on the session's own subject are skipped unless they are CONGESTION; the rest are handed to the session actor.
The subscription is aborted at once, but the departure is parked for 2 seconds. Observers skip the wait and are never announced.
Only if the session had been Active and the user did not reconnect. Published on room.ROOM.system.

connmgr.title: Inside the connection manager: the election
connmgr.sub: How the browser client goes from a list of server URLs to one active connection. Timers in connection_controller.rs drive it: probes every 200 ms, a completion check every 100 ms.
connmgr.cap: WebTransport is preferred as a class, not by latency: a slower WebTransport connection with two samples still beats a faster WebSocket one. After the election the same probes run once a second to watch for degradation. The probe body goes through the same AES step as media, so the server can recognise it as an RTT probe only while end-to-end encryption is off, which is the default.

steps.d: Open a connection to every WebSocket URL and every WebTransport URL and enter the Testing state.
Every server connection gets its own session id; ids for connections that are not elected yet are parked.
A MEDIA packet of type RTT with a monotonic timestamp, sent as a datagram where the transport has them.
Round trips outside a sane range are discarded; the last 10 are averaged per connection.
If no connection has 2 samples yet, the deadline is extended by a second, at most twice.
Lowest average RTT among WebTransport connections with at least 2 samples, then WebSocket connections with at least 2, then WebTransport and WebSocket connections with fewer.

steps.t: Start the heartbeat on the winner
steps.d: Every 5 seconds, first tick 5 seconds after the election, carrying camera, microphone, screen and speaking state. Media, health reports or an immediate heartbeat on a camera, microphone, screen or speaking change may reach the server sooner; whichever non-probe packet arrives first activates the session there.
Once a second: probe again, and start a re-election if RTT has degraded.

types.title: Inside the wire format: the protobuf messages
types.sub: Everything on a WebSocket, a WebTransport stream or a NATS subject is a serialized PacketWrapper. Its data field holds one of the other messages, chosen by packet_type.
types.cap: Control signals that must reach peers quickly (heartbeat, RTT probe, keyframe request) are media types inside a MEDIA envelope rather than envelope types of their own. With end-to-end encryption on, the data of media, heartbeat and RTT packets is ciphertext; diagnostics, health reports and the public keys still travel in the clear.

tables.name: PacketWrapper
tables.note: The envelope. Servers route on these fields; they look inside a MEDIA payload only to spot RTT probes and keyframe requests.

fields.note: RSA_PUB_KEY, AES_KEY, MEDIA, CONNECTION, DIAGNOSTICS, HEALTH, MEETING, SESSION_ASSIGNED, CONGESTION
sender's user id; a reserved system id on server-made meeting events
which connection sent it; stamped by the server if the client left it at 0

tables.name: MediaPacket
tables.note: Inside a MEDIA envelope: one encoded frame or a small control signal.

fields.note: VIDEO, AUDIO, SCREEN, HEARTBEAT, RTT, KEYFRAME_REQUEST

tables.name: VideoMetadata
tables.note: What a receiver needs to detect a gap.

fields.note: per-stream counter set by the encoder

tables.name: HeartbeatMetadata
tables.note: A peer's on/off state, sent every 5 seconds and on change.

tables.name: MeetingPacket
tables.note: Inside a MEETING envelope: lifecycle events made by the media servers and the Meeting API. Most travel on room.ROOM.system; a few are sent straight to one client.

fields.note: MEETING_STARTED, MEETING_ENDED, PARTICIPANT_JOINED, PARTICIPANT_LEFT, MEETING_ACTIVATED, PARTICIPANT_ADMITTED, PARTICIPANT_REJECTED, WAITING_ROOM_UPDATED
who the event is about; clients ignore admissions aimed at others

tables.name: HealthPacket
tables.note: Inside a HEALTH envelope: one client's view of every peer. Never relayed to the room.

fields.note: per peer: can listen, can see, NetEq and video stats

tables.name: DiagnosticsPacket
tables.note: Inside a DIAGNOSTICS envelope: a receiver's report about one sender's stream, relayed to the room.
